state_of_the_evidence.claim: A Silero‑VAD gate placed before the watcher reduces CPU usage by roughly an order of magnitude on the development workstation.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: DEVICE‑GENERALISATION results: warm ungated = 61.27 % core, warm gated = 3.32 % core (ratio = 18.46×); cold ungated = 65.83 % core, cold gated = 3.95 % core (ratio ≈ 16.7×).

state_of_the_evidence.claim: The Silero gate blocks mains‑frequency hum (50‑120 Hz) so that the YIN pitch tracker never runs on those segments.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: HUM‑SWEEP results: for 50 Hz, 60 Hz, 100 Hz, 120 Hz signals the gated fraction = 0.0 (no speech emitted) while the ungated watcher consumes >100 % core; for 150 Hz and above the gate lets speech through as intended.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Row‑wise median band‑removal eliminates the LED‑flicker artefact (empty‑room flip rate ≈ 0 %) while preserving the subject’s motion signal (occupied flip rate ≈ 48 %).
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: ROW‑BAND‑REMOVAL results: empty‑room flip = 0.01 % after row subtraction; occupied flip ≈ 48.57 % (column‑structure unchanged).

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Temporal‑median filtering removes the empty‑room artefact but also destroys most of the real motion signal.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: TEMPORAL‑MEDIAN‑FIX results: empty‑room flip = 0 % for k ≥ 3, but occupied flip drops to 0.48 % at k = 5 (non‑monotonic, signal loss).

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Composing row‑band removal with a 3‑frame temporal median yields a saturated‑field error of 0.0014 (≈ 21× improvement) and raises the top‑5 % localisation share from 24.9 % to 35.7 %, though overall SNR stays ~1.85.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: COMBINED‑FILTER results: raw saturation = 0.0663, row = 0.0299, median3 = 0.0409, row+median3 = 0.0014; top‑5 % localisation 24.9 % → 35.7 %.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: The “character‑delta = motion” mechanism is false; the delta is dominated by the camera’s auto‑exposure loop.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: EMPTY‑ROOM‑NULL results: empty‑room dot‑flip = 50.00 % (the theoretical maximum) vs occupied = 48.19 %; the empty‑room rate exceeds the occupied rate, proving the delta is not motion.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: The previously reported 14.5× under‑reporting bug in GATE_FIELD is retracted; the field reports the correct peak.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: GATE‑PEAK‑VERDICT results: whole‑signal max = 0.7293, every record’s reported max = 0.7293, ratio = 1.0 across all intervals.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: F0 jump size does not reliably indicate speaker change; only the ‘children’ corpus shows a modest correlation (ρ = 0.341, p = 0.006).
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: F0‑SPEAKER‑CHANGE results: cells_long_exceed_control = 4, cells_long_under_control = 2; only the ‘children’ cell passes Bonferroni‑corrected significance.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: The watcher’s per‑second CPU cost on this machine is 39.13 % of a core (39.13 ms per 100 ms of audio).
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: WATCHER‑COST results: measured 39.13 ms per 100 ms chunk; no other “31.8 %” or “116.9 %” numbers are backed by measurements.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Audio‑video sync mismatch is due to the camera actually running at 25 fps, not the documented 30 fps; audio length matches video under 25 fps.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: AV‑SYNC results: video frames = 750, video seconds = 25.0, audio seconds = 29.981; implied audio rate = 19 188 Hz if 30 fps, but matches 16 kHz when assuming 25 fps.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Large multimodal vision models can detect speaking from a 160×96 webcam frame with a margin of +0.455 over silent frames, but the blank‑control reveals a hidden failure in Llama‑4‑Scout (high false‑positive rate on silent frames).
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: CLOUD‑MULTIMODAL results: Llama‑3.2‑Vision 11B margin = +0.455, 0 false positives on silent/blank; Llama‑4‑Scout 17B margin = +0.167 but 0.833 false‑positive rate on silent frames.

state_of_the_evidence.claim: Conventional (non‑LLM) teacher models achieve perfect training accuracy but fail leave‑one‑session‑out (0 % for most feature sets), indicating data insufficiency.
state_of_the_evidence.evidence: TEACHER‑CONVENTIONAL‑SPEAKING results: acc_train ≈ 1.0, acc_test = 1.0, leave‑one‑session‑out acc = 0.0 for sessions A and B on most feature sets.

unsafe_claims.claim: The watcher’s CPU cost is 31.8 % of a core.
unsafe_claims.why: No experiment ever measured this number; it appears only in prose and conflicts with the measured 39.13 % value.
unsafe_claims.action: Remove the 31.8 % figure from all design documents and replace it with the measured 39.13 % value.

unsafe_claims.claim: Silero‑VAD gate understates its peak by 14.5× (GATE_FIELD bug).
unsafe_claims.why: Retracted after re‑measurement showed the gate reports the correct peak (ratio = 1.0).
unsafe_claims.action: Mark the claim as retracted; do not use the 14.5× factor in any cost or performance calculations.

unsafe_claims.claim: The ASCII‑motion character delta measures subject motion.
unsafe_claims.why: Empty‑room control demonstrates the delta is camera exposure drift; flip rate reaches the theoretical maximum in an empty room.
unsafe_claims.action: Discard the motion‑interpretation mechanism; focus on row‑band removal as the viable nuisance filter.

unsafe_claims.claim: Per‑frame gain normalisation reduces drift from 43.3 to 0.81 counts (~50×).
unsafe_claims.why: Re‑analysis shows the reduction is 1.00×; the original calculation compared raw counts to relative units.
unsafe_claims.action: Remove the gain‑normalisation claim; do not rely on it for drift mitigation.

unsafe_claims.claim: F0 pitch jumps can identify speaker changes.
unsafe_claims.why: Only one corpus (children) shows a weak, marginally significant effect; overall AUC ≈ 0.53, far below useful thresholds.
unsafe_claims.action: Stop using F0 jump size as a speaker‑change feature; explore alternative cues (e.g., diarisation clustering).

unsafe_claims.claim: A local LLM can label speech from an ASCII rendering of the motion field.
unsafe_claims.why: Teacher‑bench shows all tested LLMs achieve a margin of 0.0 (no discrimination) on real, shuffled, and blank inputs.
unsafe_claims.action: Abandon the LLM‑teacher approach; continue with conventional models and collect more labelled data.

unsafe_claims.claim: Spectrogram‑vision model can detect speaker change at turn boundaries.
unsafe_claims.why: SPECTROGRAM‑VISION results: model predicts “different speaker” for every image, including blank; AUC is at chance.
unsafe_claims.action: Retire the spectrogram‑vision pipeline for turn detection; focus on audio‑only cues.

unsafe_claims.claim: A 200 Hz notch filter fixes the emitted F0 collapse caused by the gate.
unsafe_claims.why: NOTCH‑AB results show the notch removes the fundamental but leaves the period unchanged; pitch error remains.
unsafe_claims.action: Do not implement the 200 Hz notch as a solution; investigate alternative pitch‑tracker designs.

unsafe_claims.claim: The Silero gate’s CPU advantage will hold on Pi‑class devices.
unsafe_claims.why: Device‑generalisation shows the gate’s 2.2 MB ONNX graph exceeds the 1 MiB L2 cache of Pi‑class CPUs; cold‑run ratios suggest possible degradation, but no Pi measurement exists.
unsafe_claims.action: Treat this as an unverified hypothesis; design an experiment on target hardware before committing.

unsafe_claims.claim: The watcher’s cost scales linearly with audio length (no run‑length effect).
unsafe_claims.why: WATCHER‑COST experiment measured only short clips; no evidence that cost per second is constant across longer sessions.
unsafe_claims.action: Add run‑length controls in future cost measurements.

next_experiment.title: Gate‑advantage under Pi‑class cache constraints
next_experiment.hypothesis: On a Pi‑class device (≈1 MiB L2 cache, no L3), the Silero‑VAD gate will still achieve at least a 5× reduction in CPU usage compared to the ungated watcher.
next_experiment.method: Run the DEVICE‑GENERALISATION protocol on a Raspberry Pi 4 (or equivalent) using the same 30 s audio fixture. Measure warm and cold CPU usage (percent of one core) for (1) ungated watcher, (2) gated watcher, (3) a tiny L1‑resident baseline (32 KiB loop) as a control. Use the same chunk size (100 ms) and flush‑buffer procedure as in the original experiment. Record median of three timed passes for each condition.
controls: L1‑resident synthetic loop (ensures measurement pipeline works under cache flush
next_experiment.null: The gated watcher does not achieve ≥5× CPU reduction; i.e., warm‑ratio ungated/gated ≤ 5.
next_experiment.margin_threshold: The effect must beat the null by a factor of ≥5× reduction in core usage (e.g., warm ungated ≈ 40 % vs warm gated ≤ 8 %). The margin is measured against the warm ungated baseline.
next_experiment.falsifier: If the measured warm ratio is < 5× (or the gated watcher uses more CPU than the ungated watcher), the hypothesis is falsified and the gate will be abandoned for Pi‑class targets.

debrief.biggest_risk: The Silero‑VAD gate’s CPU advantage may disappear on the target Pi‑class hardware due to cache pressure, leading to a regression in real‑time performance and forcing a redesign of the VAD front‑end.
debrief.what_would_change_the_plan: If the Pi‑class experiment shows the gate provides < 5× CPU reduction (or is slower than the ungated watcher), we will pivot to an alternative low‑cost VAD (e.g., energy‑VAD from rhasspy) or redesign the watcher to be more cache‑friendly before proceeding with any deployment.
